front.title: Simplified health cost
front.html:
For covered in-network bills B, deductible d, coinsurance c and OOP cap M:
⟨O=\min\{M,\min(B,d)+c\max(B-d,0)\}⟩
B, d, M, O are dollars; c is a decimal.
Assume no copays, all costs count toward deductible and cap, and no exclusions. Actual plans may apply separate service rules.
Annual total = 12 × monthly premium + O.

front.title: Health-plan example
front.text: Covered in-network bills $9,000; deductible $2,000; coinsurance 20%; cap $6,000; premium $210 monthly.

back.title: Which health plan wins?
head: Same covered bills
Plan A
Plan B
back.after: No copays, exclusions or network differences. A saves $1,200 with no claims; B saves $400 at $9,000 bills. Expected care and available cash affect the choice.

back.title: Worst-case budget
back.html:
For covered in-network care in the simplified plans:
⟨\text{Worst annual total}=12p+M⟩
p = monthly premium dollars; M = OOP cap.
A: $1,800 + $6,000 = $7,800
B: $3,000 + $4,000 = $7,000
Noncovered or out-of-network costs may add more. A deductible is not the same as an OOP maximum.

back.title: Expected loss
back.text: ⟨E=\sum p_jL_j⟩; p = probability (decimal), L = loss dollars. Expected value is a long-run average.
back.example: 2% chance of a $10,000 loss; otherwise no loss.
steps: One year may have $0 or $10,000 loss.

back.title: Deductible trade-off
back.html:
Suppose raising a deductible from $500 to $1,500 saves $200 yearly.
Extra risk per qualifying claim = $1,000.
⟨\dfrac{1{,}000}{200}=5⟩ years of premium savings.
This is a simple recovery-time comparison, not a prediction of claims. Consider claim frequency and whether you could pay $1,500 tomorrow. A higher deductible can fit larger reserves.

back.title: Compare the whole policy
items: Same covered risks, limits and exclusions?
How much could I owe in a bad year?
Could I pay the deductible without new debt?
Are liability limits enough for the risk?
Prioritize losses you cannot comfortably absorb; smaller predictable costs may fit your own reserves.

back.title: Reminders & mistakes
good: Premiums buy risk protection, even without a claim.
Compare both likely use and severe-loss scenarios.
bad: premiums and exclusions may not count.
